events.excerpt: European tech buyers are increasingly choosing cybersecurity vendors from their own continent in a bid to reduce their reliance on American technology. Digital sovereignty isn't only prompting enterprise customers to question their clouds of choice, it is also reshaping other parts of the industry too, and the shift is marked. According to sales figures compiled by Context, distributor sales in EMEA of cybersecurity products from EU-headquartered vendors jumped 35 percent in the two years to calendar Q3 2026. Total cybersecurity sales grew up 10 percent over the same period, and sales by US-run companies went up just 8 percent. That growth is from a relatively small base, though EU vendors gained nearly three percentage points to reach 15 percent of tracked sales by value. There is still a long way to go as US-headquartered vendors accounted for 62 percent. The trend coincides with a loss of trust in the Trump administration among customers outside of America, after it cosied up to autocratic rulers while criticizing and punishing allies with tariffs and more. Context stopped short of assigning blame. events.excerpt: A new extension brings a working global menu bar to the GNOME desktop, even for some apps that don’t have menu bars at all. Orbit Global Menu is a new GNOME extension that gives the GNOME desktop a feature it was intentionally designed without, and one that some users miss very badly – this vulture being one of them. It adds a working global menu bar to the GNOME top panel. We suspect this is something that will cause strongly contrasting opinions among many GNOME users: some will by puzzled why anyone would bother, while others may think "at last!" and rush to try it. There have been other attempts to do this before, and the Reg FOSS desk has tried several of them, but we never found one that worked with the majority of applications. Our fondness for this UI feature was visible in the two-part series we wrote in September on how to customize Xfce and then in part two how to get the global menu working with more apps. The problem is getting worse over time, as in recent versions (since GNOME 40 and Gtk4), the GNOME human-interface guidelines encourage smartphone-style hamburger menus, replacing the traditional horizontal menu bar. events.excerpt: Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where all the victims are self-owned. This week, we welcome you to a London hotel where you could check out its admin credentials for a booking website just by walking past the front desk. Our story comes courtesy of Neycho Tepavicharov, co-founder of Flashcloud, a Delaware-based web hosting company. He was staying at a hotel in London when he noticed a shocking breach of basic security protocols by management, who were a little too hospitable with their credentials. As he was passing through the lobby, Tepavicharov noticed that the door behind the front desk was open and, inside that back room, there was a whiteboard. On the whiteboard, written in plain English, were the hotel’s Booking.com administrative username and password. Anyone near the desk could clearly see the login information, and if they didn’t have time to write it down, they could have snapped a picture for later use. As Tepavicharov explains, there’s plenty of mischief you could perform with these credentials. “With that login, someone could change or cancel reservations, see guests’ names and contact details, or message guests pretending to be the hotel,” he said. “Fake 'please confirm your payment' messages sent from compromised hotel accounts are a well-known scam.” An attacker c
events.headline: London hotel put admin login for booking website on whiteboard behind the front desk

events.excerpt: I would like to discuss a wallet design built around three components: Lindell 2-of-2 MPC signing, QR-only initialization, and encrypted NFC communication between a computer and a phone. The goal is to keep the convenience of a desktop wallet while ensuring that compromising either device alone does not provide unilateral signing authority. Lindell 2-of-2 MPC as the signing foundation The computer and phone each hold a private share of one joint signing key. Neither device holds the complete private key. Using a reviewed implementation of Lindell’s two-party ECDSA protocol , both devices interact to compute a signature without revealing their shares or reconstructing the complete private key. For Ethereum, the implementation would use secp256k1 and produce one ordinary ECDSA signature under the joint public key. The wallet can therefore use a normal Ethereum address without requiring an on-chain multisignature contract. The 2-of-2 requirement comes from the signing protocol itself: obtaining the computer’s share alone is insufficient, and obtaining the phone’s share alone is also insufficient. events.excerpt: Keeping sensitive data within national borders might satisfy a residency requirement. But does it mean your organization is genuinely in control? Not necessarily. Data could be stored locally while remaining subject to another jurisdiction's laws, dependent on overseas service providers or exposed to disruption beyond your control. For enterprise IT teams, that distinction is becoming harder to ignore. Geopolitical tensions, evolving regulations and the growing use of AI are forcing organizations to reconsider what data sovereignty means in practice. Yet translating those concerns into a workable strategy is another matter. And simply throwing more money at the problem won't necessarily solve it. In The Register's on-demand webinar, Data Sovereignty By Design, moderator Tim Phillips speaks with Patrick Smith, Field CTO for EMEA at Everpure, formerly Pure Storage, about moving beyond compliance checklists and taking a more strategic approach to data control. Drawing on findings from Everpure's research, Smith explores a curious disconnect: organizations are increasing their investment in sovereignty initiatives, yet many still lack a coordinated strategy. Some of the risks attracting the most attention aren't necessarily those receiving the greatest investment. The discussion exam
events.headline: Data sovereignty takes more than keeping data close to home

events.excerpt: Every so often a flaw comes along that shows how fast the ground can shift under IT and security teams. PHP2Shell, a pair of critical flaws in PHP, was one of them. Details leaked before the planned disclosure, frontier AI helped researchers find the flaws, and PHP shipped fixes the next day. For many teams, though, the patch was the easy part. So what does it take to respond at that speed, and where should teams begin? What does governed autonomous IT look like in practice? Picture a loop. Software finds where a risk lives and ranks what matters most. It proposes a fix, then, inside limits people define, carries it out and checks that it worked. Routine, low-risk actions can run on their own. Higher-impact ones wait for a person to approve. A few are never handed over at all. Each step leaves a record that someone can review and reverse. What challenges do IT and security teams face today? Three problems keep coming up. The first is visibility. PHP2Shell reportedly sat undetected for more than a decade. For these two flaws, the fix was a version upgrade. The hard part was finding every copy of PHP, including copies bundled inside other software or extracted by hand onto Windows machines that never registered as installed applications. events.excerpt: Disclosure: I am the creator of Atomic Ownership Blockchains (AOB), which this repo covers in more detail than the other designs. What this is An open-source skill (SKILL.md format, Apache-2.0) that lets LLM agents analyze blockchain architectures on several independent dimensions instead of one number. The Nakamoto coefficient is a single-subsystem snapshot, goes stale, and is not comparable across consensus mechanisms, so the skill treats it as one input per subsystem, not a ranking. Dimensions currently covered: Node/validator concentration (NC per subsystem), stake/wealth concentration (Gini/HHI), client diversity, network/infrastructure Consensus dependency scope: does finalizing this transaction need agreement from parties unrelated to it? Privileged actors, payment finality authority, reliance on economic assumptions Sybil exposure, blast radius of one attack or one lost key, eclipse/network-view attacks, cost to participate It compares PoW, PoS, DAG, sharded designs and AOB, and reports each design’s validation level (production history, audits, testnet) separately from what its architecture does.
